subject: computer processor chip
title: What If Your Computer Got Division Wrong? In 1994 Millions Did

scenes.text: What if your computer couldn't divide properly? In 1994, millions couldn't, and one maths professor noticed.
Thomas Nicely was hunting prime numbers on a brand-new Intel Pentium when his totals came out wrong. His older computer disagreed.
The chip's division circuit used a lookup table of about a thousand entries. Five had been left blank. Some divisions came back wrong in the fourth decimal place.
Intel said a typical user would hit the bug once in 27,000 years. IBM said once every 24 days, and stopped shipping Pentium PCs.
Intel first offered new chips only to people who could prove they needed one. The jokes and headlines got louder for weeks.
On December 20th, 1994, Intel gave in: a free chip for anyone who asked. The bill: about 475 million dollars, for five missing numbers.

description:
What if your computer got division wrong? In 1994 millions of Intel Pentium processors did.
Mathematics professor Thomas Nicely of Lynchburg College discovered the flaw while computing prime numbers: five entries were missing from the chip's roughly 1,000-entry division lookup table, so certain divisions returned wrong digits from about the fourth decimal place. Intel estimated an average user would meet the error once in 27,000 years; IBM estimated once every 24 days and halted Pentium PC shipments. After weeks of public pressure, Intel announced a no-questions-asked replacement programme on 20 December 1994 and took a charge of about 475 million dollars.
